executive_summary: NZD/USD closed at 0.56319 on Friday 30 October 2026. That is the number of US dollars per New Zealand dollar, so a rising pair means a stronger kiwi. The pair is up 0.48% over one month, down 4.47% over three months, down 5.14% over six months and down 0.47% over a year. It sits at the 10th percentile of its 52-week closing range, 55 pips above the midpoint of the five-touch 0.5556-0.5598 support band. The bilateral story is a split between the two central banks. The RBNZ held at 2.75% on 28 October by a 4-3 vote, with a dovish majority. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% the same day by 10-2, with both dissents favouring a hike. The policy gap stays at -112.5bp, and the two-year gap is about -81bp. Both banks are priced at about three-in-four odds to hike on 9 December, but the New Zealand odds are the more fragile on data. That fragility, the oil shock to New Zealand's terms of trade, the 7 November election and year-end dollar funding tightness are the bilateral edge. None of them shows up clearly in either currency's standalone view. The tactical stance is Bearish, conviction 3 (net weighted score -0.333), with a four-week base case of 0.5580 by 27 November. The strategic stance is Neutral, conviction 2 (+0.024), because both rate paths are overpriced by similar amounts and both are tested on the same day. The caveat is location. The speculative kiwi short is near a five-year extreme and spot sits just above major support, so the better tactical entry is selling a rebound into 0.5660-0.5690, not selling at spot.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Both dossiers use the same World Bank PPP anchor of NZD/USD 0.6789. That puts the kiwi 17% below parity, or equivalently the dollar 20.5% rich against it. In real effective terms the BIS index for New Zealand is 100.15 (September 2026), 2.07 points lower over a year. The US index is 107.11, at the 21st percentile of its range since January 2024. So the dollar is not expensive in trade-weighted real terms, but the kiwi is cheap. Westpac notes the NZ dollar is at a 17-year low in trade-weighted terms. The current level prices an oil-driven hit to New Zealand's terms of trade and a dollar that keeps its yield premium. It does not price a Gulf settlement. Valuation is a long-run anchor that limits how much downside is left, not a catalyst within four weeks. The 52-week range on closes is 0.55857 (12 October) to 0.60657 (spot at the 10th percentile); on an intraday basis it is 0.5566-0.6093 (13th percentile).

market_context.recent_regime: The pair has moved from a trending decline (August to mid-October) to a range-bound pause just above the year's low. Three things kept it there: the RBNZ's surprise hold, a Fed that leans hawkish, and Brent's roughly 15% October rise to US$117.64. Before the RBNZ decision the market was close to fully priced for a hike: tightening was nearly fully discounted in money markets, making the hold a huge surprise. The pair fell from 0.5686 to an intraday 0.55839 before stabilising near 0.5630. The dollar leg has been firm through rate differentials rather than safe-haven demand. The kiwi leg is now trading on the 4 November labour data, the 7 November election and positioning.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Holding NZD/USD long earns -112.5bp a year: the OCR of 2.75% less the Fed funds midpoint of 3.875%. Against the CME 3-month at-the-money implied volatility of 8.193% (98.7-day tenor), the carry-to-volatility ratio is -0.137. The futures market shows a premium of about 117.5bp a year, measured between the December 2026 and March 2027 CME kiwi futures. By covered interest parity that figure is the interest differential plus the cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated, so it is not the policy differential. Carry works in the dollar's favour, but only modestly. A ratio of -0.14 is too small to attract or repel much capital on its own, so carry is a mild headwind for the pair rather than a driver. It would worsen if the Fed hikes on 9 December and the RBNZ does not, and would be roughly unchanged if both hike. Forward points are indicative, applying the 117.5bp futures premium to spot.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The policy gap is 112.5bp against the kiwi. The OCR is 2.75% after the RBNZ's 4-3 hold on 28 October. The Fed funds mid-point is 3.875% after the Fed's 10-2 hold on the same day, in which Cook and Hammack voted for a hike. Neither bank decides again inside the four-week window. Both announce on 9 December, the RBNZ with a Monetary Policy Statement and the Fed with projections, so the gap is fixed until then. The tactical question is how each side's December pricing moves on data. Markets price the two banks about the same (about 76% for an RBNZ hike, 77-85% for a Fed hike), but the committees behind those odds differ. The RBNZ majority held because household demand is weak, and committee member Hansen calls December 50-50, while the Fed's dissent leans hawkish. That makes New Zealand's short-end yields the more fragile of the two. The 2-year NZGB at 3.80% sits 81bp below the 2-year Treasury at 4.61% (both 29 October). The 4 November labour data can cut RBNZ odds more easily than US payrolls on 6 November or CPI on 10 November can cut the Fed's, given 3.4% annualised Q3 growth and 3.1% core PCE in the US. The effect reaches the pair through the 2-year spread and the carry: a kiwi holder pays 112.5bp a year, and the dollar side of the futures roll earns about 117.5bp.

tactical.what_is_priced: Both curves price a December hike at nearly the same odds, so the static differential is priced. What is not priced is that the RBNZ's dovish majority makes its odds the more likely to fall on soft data before 9 December. That asymmetry, not a change in the differential, is the bearish edge.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both banks are expected to hike once more, to 3.00% and 4.00-4.25%. That keeps the gap at about 87.5-125bp and roughly where it is now. Both markets also price more tightening than the central banks are likely to deliver. New Zealand overnight index swaps priced about 4.1% for December 2027 on 7 October, against a likely RBNZ peak of 3.25-3.50% and a stated neutral range of 3-3.5%. US futures price close to 4.7% by September 2027, against a median dot of 4.1%. The two overpricings are of similar size, 50-75bp in New Zealand and about 60bp in the US, and both get their first test on the same day, 9 December, when the Statement track and the dot plot are published together. The RBNZ has one more confirmed decision inside the horizon, the 10 February Review. No further FOMC date is confirmed before March, which gives the RBNZ a slightly earlier chance to narrow the gap. The transmission is the expected path of the 2-year spread. With both paths likely to be repriced lower by similar amounts, the factor carries no clear direction for the pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Growth favours the US. Q3 US GDP rose 3.4% annualised (0.83% q/q), and the October flash composite PMI was 57.6. New Zealand grew 0.25% q/q in Q2, with household consumption up only 0.1% and real national disposable income down 0.4%. Inflation is similar on core measures: New Zealand's trimmed mean is 3.0% and weighted median 3.1%, against US core PCE of 3.1%. Headline is 3.7% in both, and New Zealand's Q3 headline undershot the RBNZ's 3.9% forecast. Labour slack differs a lot. New Zealand unemployment is 5.6%, a decade high, while US unemployment is 4.2%, though US payroll growth has slowed to 29,000 in September. The window holds New Zealand's Q3 labour data on 4 November, US payrolls on 6 November and US CPI on 10 November. The US prints are more likely to keep the Fed on course than New Zealand's are to revive RBNZ conviction. The effect reaches the pair through each side's December hike odds, and the growth gap points those odds against the kiwi.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both economies face oil-driven headline inflation, but they absorb it differently. The RBNZ projects New Zealand CPI at 4.4% in Q4 on fuel, while household saving is 3.7%, house prices fall and Westpac has cut 2026 growth to 2.5%. That is a squeeze on real incomes, and the RBNZ majority signalled it would largely look through it. The US is a net energy exporter whose growth is led by investment and productivity. Even if US growth slows towards 2%, it stays ahead of a New Zealand economy whose terms of trade fell 9.0% in Q2. The US weak spot is the labour market: real earnings are down 0.7% y/y and payroll growth averages about 51,000 over three months. A jump in US unemployment towards 4.5% is the main thing that could reverse this factor. The effect reaches the pair through the relative policy reaction: inflation from fuel costs that one bank looks through, against demand that keeps the other alert.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The kiwi is a high-beta risk currency and the dollar is the funding and reserve currency. Usually that makes risk-off moves bearish for the pair, but this regime adds an oil channel that hits only one side. The VIX closed at 17.2 on 29 October and traded near 20 the next day. US high-yield spreads widened 18bp in a month to 326bp. Investors expect possible US strikes on Iran once the 3 November midterms are over. A strike that pushes Brent higher would hurt New Zealand twice, through wider risk premia and a larger fuel import bill, while the US as a net energy exporter takes no terms-of-trade hit. The offset is that the dollar's haven response is weak at present: the dollar index slipped on the 30 October equity sell-off as the yen and franc took the haven flows. A risk-off shock therefore hurts the kiwi more reliably than it helps the dollar. The most likely shock in the window still pushes the pair lower.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the risk channel is two-sided for this pair. A negotiated Gulf settlement, which Qatari mediators were pursuing on 30 October, would cut oil and lift equities together. That is the rare case where both of the kiwi's external channels improve while the dollar loses its terms-of-trade advantage over energy importers. Escalation would do the opposite. A third path is a correction in US equities led by AI-related stocks, which is US-centric. ING flags low hedge ratios on US assets as the main risk to the dollar, so such a correction could weaken the dollar through hedging flows even as risk-off weighs on the kiwi. The dossiers weight settlement, persistent disruption and slowdown roughly equally. None of the three dominates, and their effects on the two legs partly offset, so the factor is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, positioning and structural flows both lean towards the pair rising, though neither is a catalyst on its own. The asset-manager short in the kiwi, the larger part of the total, mostly reflects hedging of New Zealand assets and real-money underweights. Its first reduction in late October suggests the hedging wave may have peaked. On the dollar side, the IMF's reserve data show the dollar's share of allocated reserves falling to 56.70% in Q2 from 57.18%. Foreign holders of US assets run low hedge ratios, and those ratios tend to rise as the Fed nears the end of its cycle, which means selling dollars forward without selling the assets. Strong private buying of US securities, USD 300.7bn net in August, is the offset. Both forces are slow. The extreme kiwi short limits how far bad news can push the pair, and dollar hedging adds slow supply of dollars.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two current account deficits are similar: 3.26% of GDP for New Zealand and 3.0% for the US (both Q2). The terms-of-trade shock, however, hits only one side. New Zealand's goods terms of trade fell 9.0% in Q2 as import prices rose 13.8%. Its September merchandise deficit of NZ$1.97bn was far wider than the NZ$775m expected. The US is a net energy exporter, so Brent at US$117.64 improves its terms of trade. Direct bilateral trade is too small to matter: on IMF data New Zealand exported US$5.5bn of goods to the US in 2024 and imported US$4.9bn, a surplus of about US$0.5bn. Dairy is the kiwi's offset, with the GDT index up 1.2% and 2.5% at the two October auctions. But peak New Zealand milk supply limits further gains, and the October trade data due on 18 November carry a full month of higher oil prices. Over four weeks oil, not dairy, sets the marginal change.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the external picture is balanced. New Zealand's deficit of 3.26% of GDP is about half the 5-7% it has historically run, and the Q2 goods surplus of NZ$1.57bn shows the export base earning. Fonterra raised its milk price midpoint to $9.50/kgMS, and Westpac forecasts $9.75. On the US side, the current account deficit is widening, the investment position fell USD 1.15tn in a quarter to -USD 22.42tn, and the twin deficits make financing more rate-sensitive as the Fed's lead narrows. Oil is the swing factor. A backwardated Brent curve implies some easing even without a settlement, while a prolonged Hormuz disruption would keep New Zealand's terms of trade depressed. Valuation is a slow anchor that favours the kiwi: its BIS real effective rate fell 2.07 points over a year to 100.15, while the dollar is rich against the kiwi on purchasing power parity. Neither side has a clear external advantage over this horizon.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar funding is tightening into year-end, and the kiwi is among the most exposed G10 currencies. Reserve balances fell USD 68.8bn in the week to 28 October to a weekly average of USD 2,893.8bn. Over the same week the Treasury General Account rose above USD 1tn, ahead of a USD 850bn end-December target. SOFR printed 3.94% on 29 October, 4bp above interest on reserve balances. The Fed's balance sheet is flat and reserve management purchases have been zero since mid-August, so nothing is offsetting the drain. New Zealand runs a current account deficit of 3.26% of GDP that needs steady foreign funding, and the RBNZ has no standing swap line with the Fed. Tighter and dearer dollars therefore raise the kiwi's funding cost more than those of larger or surplus currencies. Central bank swap-line use of USD 156m shows tightness rather than stress, which is why confidence is modest.

Election history also argues for patience: Westpac's analysis shows the NZ dollar weakens on average from around 10 days before an election and recovers for around 10 days after. The reading is genuinely balanced, not low-conviction directional. Both sides' rate paths are overpriced by similar amounts and both get their first test on the same day. Mapping to conviction: at +0.024 the score is inside the ±0.10 band, so the stance is Neutral; conviction is 2.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights, Policy & Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.16), Guidance (0.12) and USD Liquidity (0.12) dominate, and all four are Neutral for this pair, leaving a net weighted score of +0.024. The dossiers partly cancel at this horizon. The kiwi dossier is Bearish at -0.16, largely because the RBNZ's December track is likely to undershoot pricing. The dollar dossier leans Bearish on the dollar at -0.096, because the Fed's path is also overpriced and the US external and fiscal positions are deteriorating. Taken bilaterally, the two overpricings mirror each other. New Zealand swaps price about four hikes against a likely RBNZ peak of 3.25-3.50%, and US futures price near 4.7% for late 2027 against a 4.1% median dot. Both are tested on 9 December, when the RBNZ Statement and the FOMC projections land together. The remaining signals offset. US growth outpacing an oil-squeezed New Zealand economy subtracts. The extreme kiwi short, slow dollar hedging and reserve diversification, and a weaker US fiscal trajectory add. What is priced is two hawkish paths and persistent Gulf disruption. The expected edge is limited to relative repricing on 9 December, which on current evidence is symmetric. The path of least resistance is therefore no strong fundamental drift for the pair beyond the one-month tactical window. The tail risks are two-sided: a Gulf settlement would help the kiwi through oil and risk together, while a Labour-led government with a dual RBNZ mandate would weigh on it. The key dates are 9 December (RBNZ Statement and FOMC projections), the 11 December US funding deadline, and the 10 February RBNZ Review, the only other confirmed decision before March. Conviction is 2 because the Neutral call reflects real offsetting forces rather than missing evidence. Either 9 December track diverging from pricing by more than the other would move this horizon decisively.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically NZD/USD is a mid-table opportunity rather than a standout. The kiwi dossier ranks the kiwi 9th of 11 and the dollar dossier ranks the dollar 6th, a narrow spread. Short USD/JPY, short USD/SEK and long USD against the euro or sterling all screen as clearer dollar trades over one to three months. Among kiwi crosses, long AUD/NZD expresses the kiwi's relative weakness more cleanly than NZD/USD, because it isolates the Antipodean rate gap from the dollar's own structural headwinds.

From January to April the pair should trade a 0.5500-0.5800 range, checked by the January Q4 CPI and the 10 February RBNZ Review. Rallies should stall first at the 0.58105-0.58255 band and the 200-day near 0.5832, then decisively at the 0.5884-0.5930 cluster as the 200-week descends into it. consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: ING's forecasts were published on 12 October, before the RBNZ's 4-3 hold on 28 October revealed a dovish majority, before Brent's roughly 15% October rise to US$117.64, and before US Q3 GDP printed 3.4% annualised. ING leans on the kiwi's undervaluation and on the RBNZ resuming hikes. We accept both, but weigh more heavily the relative fragility of New Zealand rate pricing against a Fed whose dissent is hawkish, the oil channel that hits only the kiwi side, and the 7 November election tail, which no located forecast addresses. Strategically we agree with ING that the dollar faces headwinds as both rate paths reprice, which is why we are Neutral rather than Bearish. We see no fundamental case for the appreciation those forecasts project.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the tactical view is right, a short-dated kiwi short against the dollar gains from the pair falling and from the dollar side of the forward roll (about 117.5bp a year) while consensus longs pay carry. In price terms that is about 52 pips plus 5 pips of roll from spot over a month, or about 95 pips from the preferred 0.5675 entry.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If ING is right, the crowded kiwi short accelerates the move against a bearish position, most likely triggered by a firm 4 November labour print, a clean coalition win or a Gulf settlement. A strategic Neutral would miss a valuation-led recovery. At spot, a move to ING's 0.57 costs a short 68 pips; the preferred 0.5745 stop caps it at 70 pips from entry.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Tactically, the window before 9 December holds no decision from either central bank. It does hold soft-looking New Zealand data, firm-looking US data, the New Zealand election, the possible strike period after the midterms and a year-end dollar funding squeeze, all of which lean against the kiwi. Strategically, the weight shifts to the two policy tracks published together on 9 December, both likely to undershoot hawkish pricing by similar amounts, and to slower forces (an extreme kiwi short, dollar hedging and US fiscal strain) that offset New Zealand's weaker growth.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: 9 December 2026, when the RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement and the FOMC Summary of Economic Projections are released the same day. Year-end funding pressure should fade in early January, and the RBNZ's 10 February Review is the next confirmed test.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Treat the bearish view as a time-limited lean running into 9 December, sized for a short-covering squeeze given the crowded kiwi short. Reassess both horizons once the two tracks are published. A track that diverges from pricing on one side only would be the trigger for a strategic directional call. In practice: sell a rebound into 0.5660-0.5690 with a 0.5745 stop; take most profit in the 0.5600-0.5560 support band; be flat or nearly flat into 9 December; after that, run strategic risk as range trading between roughly 0.5500 and 0.5900 unless one track diverges.

catalysts.event: US midterm elections; opening of the window for possible US strikes on Iran
catalysts.rationale: A Democratic House is about 94% priced, so the result itself should move the dollar little. The bigger issue is that the President said there would be no strikes on Iran before the vote. A strike would lift oil and widen risk premia, hurting the kiwi as an oil importer and high-beta currency far more than the energy-exporting dollar.

After gains of 1.2% and 2.5% at the two October auctions, a third rise would support New Zealand's export income and the milk price outlook, and could set off short covering in a crowded kiwi short. Peak-season New Zealand milk supply limits how far prices can rise, so a flat result is equally plausible.

catalysts.event: New Zealand Q3 labour market (household labour force survey, labour cost index)
catalysts.rationale: This is the release most able to move RBNZ December odds before 9 December. Unemployment at 5.5-5.6% with muted wages would trim the roughly 76% pricing towards 60% and weigh on the pair. A fall to 5.3% or below would lift odds and could force covering of the 57,690-contract kiwi short. Wages matter as much as the headline: a better employment headline with subdued wages would offer less support for an earlier RBNZ move. Bank of New Zealand forecasts third-quarter employment growth of 0.4% and an unemployment rate of 5.6%.

Consensus is +55,000 payrolls and 4.2% unemployment. A print near consensus keeps Fed December odds of 77-85% intact and supports the dollar's yield and funding advantage. A negative print with higher unemployment would cut those odds and is the main dollar-side risk to the bearish view.

Polls give the governing coalition 61 seats only if the overhang stays small, and the dossier puts a hung or delayed result at 40%. Uncertainty pending special votes would hold a risk premium on the kiwi, and a change of government brings a possible dual RBNZ mandate. Because the vote is on a Saturday, the first reaction arrives as a gap at the Monday open. Bank economists see an asymmetric reaction: CBA expects the kiwi to rise modestly if the current coalition wins, while a Labour-led coalition with substantial Green leverage could weigh on the currency.

September core CPI ran at a 3.4% three-month annualised pace, with headline at 3.7% on energy. Another 0.3% monthly core print would cement the Fed's December hike and the dollar's front-end premium over New Zealand, pushing the pair lower. A soft print would be a dollar-negative surprise.

The second November auction tests whether the October rally in whole milk powder holds as New Zealand milk supply peaks. A cumulative gain of several percent across November would partly offset the oil hit to New Zealand's terms of trade, while a fall would reinforce it.

catalysts.event: New Zealand October merchandise trade; FOMC minutes of the 27-28 October meeting
catalysts.rationale: October's trade data include a roughly 15% rise in Brent, so another deficit near September's NZ$1.97bn would confirm the terms-of-trade drag. The same day, the Fed's minutes could show hawkish support beyond the two dissents, which would lift December odds. Both point lower for the pair.

catalysts.event: RBNZ OCR decision with Monetary Policy Statement; FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: Both banks are about three-in-four priced to hike, and both publish projections on the same day. The pair will move on which track undershoots its market pricing by more: an RBNZ track peaking well below the roughly four priced hikes would weigh on the kiwi, while dots confirming a hold through 2027 would weigh on the dollar.

catalysts.event: Expiry of the continuing resolution funding the US government
catalysts.rationale: A lapse in funding would delay US data and raise fiscal risk premia on US assets without lifting policy expectations. That combination weighs on the dollar, and it would lift the pair against a dollar that has otherwise been supported by year-end funding demand.

catalysts.event: RBNZ OCR decision with Monetary Policy Review
catalysts.rationale: This is the RBNZ's only other confirmed decision before March and the test of whether it follows its December track with a second hike. No FOMC decision is confirmed between 9 December and March, so this meeting gives New Zealand an unopposed chance to move the differential.

assumptions: Price series: the analysis uses daily closing prices, 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30, with spot 0.56319 at the 30 October close. Moving averages and support and resistance zones are computed over the full history of 4,919 weekday sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30, which yields 1,010 weekly and 462 monthly bars. The 50-, 100- and 200-day and the 200-week averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. The 200-week slope is measured per week. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR(14) is 43 pips. Zones are clusters of weekly and monthly swing closes with stated touch counts. Distances are measured from spot to each zone's midpoint, in pips and as a percentage of spot.

Data quality: only ten resistance zones and two support zones met the two-touch threshold. The support list is therefore supplemented with the round numbers 0.5500 and 0.5450, which have no touch history in the record. The 52-week range is reported on both intraday (0.5566-0.6093, spot at the 13th percentile) and closing (0.55857-0.60657, 10th percentile) bases, and the closing basis is used in prose.

Spot date and valuation date: the 30 October spot predates the 1 November valuation date only by a weekend with no trading sessions in between. A Monday 2 November quote near 0.5626 was seen in research but is not used. Every level, pip distance and percentage is anchored to 0.56319.

Rates and yields: the policy differential is -112.5bp: OCR 2.75%, confirmed by the 28 October hold, against the 3.875% midpoint of the Fed's 3.75-4.00% range. The ten-year yields in the monthly series are September 2026 averages (New Zealand 4.94%, US 4.99%) and are not live levels. The daily closes quoted are NZGB 4.90% and UST 4.98% on 29 October, with two-year yields of 3.80% and 4.61%. New Zealand December pricing (about 76%) is a summary of trader pricing after the decision. The full New Zealand OIS path (4.1% by December 2027) dates from 7 October, before the hold.

Volatility and funding: the 3-month implied volatility of 8.193% is the CME at-the-money quote at the 98.7-day quarterly tenor observed on 29 October, not a 90-day interpolation, and it is the carry-to-volatility denominator. The implied-volatility percentile is not used because quotes exist only since late August, so it is null in the structured output. The roughly 117.5bp futures premium is the annualised spread between the December 2026 and March 2027 CME kiwi futures. It combines the interest differential and the cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated, and no free source publishes NZD/USD cross-currency basis. Forward points are therefore indicative.

Positioning and trade: CFTC positioning is for the week to 27 October 2026. Kiwi percentiles and the five-year range are computed from CFTC history. Bilateral goods trade figures are IMF Direction of Trade Statistics for 2024, used as given. The dollar-side CFTC percentile in the structured output (57) is the dollar-index five-year percentile.

Weights and scoring: default weights apply except Factor 4 (+0.03 tactical, +0.02 strategic) and Factor 9 (-0.03 tactical, -0.02 strategic). This reflects positioning at a five-year extreme and an options-only Factor 9 whose skew is already counted under positioning. Net stance follows the score mechanically (Bearish at or below -0.10, Neutral inside ±0.10). The factor scores rest on rates, macro data, policy communication, positioning, trade, geopolitics, valuation and cross-asset evidence. They exclude the pair's own recent trading, which is used only for levels, entries, stops, sizing, scenario targets and the price-action narrative.

Probabilities and calendar: central bank, election and geopolitical probabilities are the dossiers' own estimates unless stated as market pricing. Scenario and invalidator probabilities are this analysis's judgements. The confirmed decision calendar between 1 November 2026 and 1 March 2027 lists 9 December (RBNZ and FOMC) and 10 February (RBNZ) only; no further FOMC date is treated as confirmed in that period.

Consensus: consensus rests on bank research (ING of 12 October and Westpac of 19-26 October, plus OCBC's and Crédit Agricole's level commentary). Model-based forecast sites are reported as sentiment only.
